The second segment, d1a14h2 (chain H residues 1-8), is not a native protein domain. It is a short non-native piece at the N-terminus of the engineered NC10 antibody heavy chain in the PDB 1a14 complex with influenza neuraminidase. It is most likely an expression or purification tag or a construct linker. SCOPe 2.08 places such segments in class l (Artifacts), fold/superfamily/family l.1.1.1 (Tags). That classification records an artifact of how the protein was made. It is not an evolutionary assignment and implies no fold, superfamily or family relationship with anything else.

The real protein domain is d1a14h1 (residues 9-111). It is an immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable domain: class b (all-beta), fold b.1 (immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich), superfamily b.1.1 (immunoglobulin), family b.1.1.1 (V set domains, antibody variable domain-like). Homology inferences for chain H should be based on d1a14h1 only.

Similarity to d1a14h2 should not be treated as evidence of protein homology. Common tags such as His-tags, linkers and leftover cleavage-site residues appear in many unrelated constructs. Any match to them reflects shared lab methods, not shared ancestry. The segment is also only 8 residues long and has low complexity, so any alignment score would be statistically meaningless. It has no function that could be transferred, and it should not be used as a structural template or chosen as a representative domain.

In practice, mask or remove class l tag segments before sequence or structure searches, clustering or benchmark construction. Hits caused only by tag residues should be counted as false positives. Choose representatives from the native domain (d1a14h1). If you are unsure whether a terminal segment is a tag, check the expression construct described in the PDB SEQADV or construct records against the UniProt sequence. That check is needed evidence, but it does not establish homology by itself.

Limitation: I could not check the exact residues of 1-8 or the construct details in this setting, so the precise tag type is not confirmed. The SCOPe artifact classification is what matters for the conclusion.
